types.name: Asset
types.doc:
Base class for all assets in the Asset Pipeline.
Inherits RefCounted for automatic lifetime management via Ref<T>.
Two-phase loading: Load() for CPU data (any thread), CreateGPU() for GPU resources (main thread).

members.name: GetAssetType
members.doc: Type identification

members.name: Load
members.doc:
Load CPU-side data. Can be called from any thread.
Returns true on success.

members.name: PrimaryLoadFile
members.signature: virtual std::string PrimaryLoadFile(const std::string& path) const
members.doc:
The one file whose bytes Load(path) reads first and whole, for a loader
that reads them through the IO queue and hands them to LoadFromMemory.
Empty (the default): Load does its own IO, and the loader only gives it
a slot on the completion pool.

members.name: LoadFromMemory
members.signature: virtual bool LoadFromMemory(const std::string& path, const std::string& file, std::vector<uint8_t>&& bytes)
members.doc: Load(path) with `file`'s bytes already read. Any thread, like Load.

members.name: Unload
members.doc: Release CPU-side data.

members.name: CreateGPU
members.doc:
Create GPU resources on the main thread.
Returns true on success.

members.name: CreateGPUBudgeted
members.signature: virtual bool CreateGPUBudgeted(const GPUContext& ctx, int budget)
members.doc:
Time-sliced GPU creation for the async-import drain. MAIN THREAD
ONLY. Does up to `budget` GPU work units (<= 0 = unbounded / one-shot).
Returns true once the asset reached a TERMINAL state — GPUReady on
success or Invalid on failure — and false while more budgeted work
remains for a following frame. The default is one-shot (a single
CreateGPU); large assets (meshes) override it to yield across frames.

members.name: EstimatedMemoryUsage
members.doc:
Estimated CPU+GPU footprint for the eviction policy.
0 = negligible / unknown (never triggers eviction by itself).

members.name: EstimatedUploadBytes
members.doc:
Bytes the remaining GPU creation will still upload, read BEFORE
CreateGPU so the per-frame drain can meter in bytes. The default is the
footprint estimate, which a texture knows from its CPU data alone; a
type whose estimate needs its GPU objects (a mesh) overrides it.

members.name: DestroyGPU
members.doc: Destroy GPU resources. Must be called on main thread.

members.name: DestroyGPUIsFrameSafe
members.doc:
True when DestroyGPU only drops RHI objects whose backends already hold
their release until the frames in flight have retired (images do, on
every backend). A reimport of such an asset needs the render thread
fenced, not the whole device drained — the drain was a multi-second
freeze in a Debug editor each time an artist saved a texture.

members.name: CanAdoptLoadedState
members.doc:
Off-thread reimport. The object a scene holds has to survive a reimport,
so the loader cannot simply hand back a new one: it parses into a fresh
object of the same type and the main thread moves that CPU state into
the live one, after Unload and before CreateGPU. A type that cannot say
which of its members Load fills keeps the synchronous reimport.

members.name: SaveMetadata
members.doc: Save import settings to a .mdfmeta MDF file

members.name: LoadMetadata
members.doc: Load import settings from a .mdfmeta MDF file

members.name: WriteImportSettings
members.doc: Override in derived classes to write type-specific import settings

members.name: ReadImportSettings
members.doc: Override in derived classes to read type-specific import settings

members.name: CollectDependencyIDs
members.doc:
Override to report the UUIDs of assets this asset references (e.g. a
material → its textures + parent). The registry stores these so it can
answer "what does X need" and the reverse "who needs X" for delete-safety
and a reference viewer. Default: no dependencies.

members.name: GetSourceHash
members.doc:
Source content hash (FNV-1a 64) + mtime, persisted in the .mdfmeta so
a project re-open restores them without re-reading every source file —
change detection works immediately and there's no reimport storm.

types.name: EAssetDropRefusal
types.doc:
Why a content-browser drag could not place what it was carrying. The drag
cursor and the drop itself both resolve through Classify, so the cursor can
never promise a spawn the release then declines — and every value but None
carries the sentence the editor shows, because a drop that evaporates in
silence reads as a broken editor rather than as a refusal.

types.name: FAssetActionPolicy
types.doc:
The policy behind the three gestures the content browser performs on a file
it did not author: dragging it into a level, opening it, and falling back to
the read-only text viewer. It lives in Game rather than in the editor so the
self-test host can pin it — the editor is an executable and nothing can link
its decisions.

members.name: IsPlaceableInLevel
members.doc:
Asset kinds a level can hold as an actor: any mesh the importer reads
(source or cooked), a prefab, and a Visual Script class.

members.name: ClassifyDrop
members.signature: static EAssetDropRefusal ClassifyDrop(const std::string& assetPath, bool haveScene, bool editing, bool overTarget)
members.doc:
`overTarget` is the viewport-or-outliner test; the caller owns it because
only the editor knows its own panel rectangles.

members.name: DropRefusalDetail
members.signature: static std::string DropRefusalDetail(EAssetDropRefusal refusal, const std::string& assetPath)

members.name: OpenNeedsLiveImport
members.doc:
Source models carry no container header, so their editor rebuilds the
whole mesh — parse, LODs, meshlets, SDF, GPU upload — to show a preview.
On the UI thread that is minutes of a frozen window for a large file, so
the open has to go through the async importer first.

members.name: IsTextViewable
members.signature: static bool IsTextViewable(const std::string& assetPath, uint64_t sizeBytes)
members.doc:
The read-only text viewer is the last resort for a file nothing claims.
A `.gltf` is JSON and an `.obj` is plain text, so a byte scan calls both
documents and hands the artist a megabyte of vertex records instead of
saying the model has no editor — the extension decides, not the bytes.

members.name: MaxTextViewBytes
members.doc:
Past this the viewer truncates anyway, and reading the rest only to throw
it away is what made opening a large file feel like a hang.

types.name: FAssetAuditRow
types.doc:
One row of the Asset Audit table: everything a licensee asks about an asset
before a ship review, in one record.

The byte counts are NOT measured here. They come out of
FAssetDependencySizes, the same pass the Size Map draws, so a figure the
treemap shows and a figure the table shows can never disagree — the audit
that grew its own stat() walk was the second answer nobody could reconcile
with the first.

members.name: referencesIn
members.doc:
Direct edges only. A transitive count would make every row in a chain
read as heavily referenced and hide the one asset that actually holds
the chain up.

members.name: modifiedTime
members.doc:
Seconds since the epoch, from the source file on disk. Zero when the
file is gone — which is itself a finding, so the row survives rather
than being dropped.

members.name: triangles
members.doc: From the package's registry tag; -1 for a type that has none.

members.name: notes
members.doc:
What the audit would act on ("Exceeds platform max size"), and how
loudly: 0 a remark, 1 a warning, 2 an error.

members.name: query
members.doc: Case-insensitive substring over name and path.

members.name: types
members.doc: Empty means every type.

members.name: folder
members.doc: Project-relative prefix, empty for the whole registry.

members.name: unreferencedOnly
members.doc:
"What can I delete": nothing points at it. Held separately from the
query so a search inside the unreferenced set stays possible.

members.name: ids
members.doc:
The audit set (UE5's Asset Audit adds assets to it): with restrictToIds
only these rows are kept; without it, the whole registry.

members.name: textureMaxSize
members.doc: The target platform's largest texture edge; 0 skips the check.

members.name: registeredAssets
members.doc:
Before the filter, so the header can say "812 of 4,913" instead of
pretending the filtered set is the project.

members.name: archivePath
members.doc:
Empty when no cooked archive backed the disk figures, which is what
turns every one of them from a shipped size into a source-file size.

members.name: Build
members.signature: static FAssetAuditReport Build(const AssetRegistry& registry, const FAssetSizeOptions& options, const FAssetAuditFilter& filter)
members.doc:
The whole registry, sized through FAssetDependencySizes and joined with
the registry's own reference counts. `options` is the size layer's own
option block: projectRoot and archivePath are the only fields that
apply, since an audit row is one asset and never a closure.

members.name: PassesFilter
members.signature: static bool PassesFilter(const FAssetAuditRow& row, const FAssetAuditFilter& filter)

members.name: Annotate
members.signature: static void Annotate(FAssetAuditRow& row, const std::vector<std::pair<std::string, std::string>>& tags, int32_t textureMaxSize)
members.doc:
Triangles and the Notes column from the package's registry tags: a
missing source, a texture over the platform's edge, a mesh missing its
textures, nothing referencing the asset — the worst one wins.

members.name: Sort
members.signature: static void Sort(std::vector<FAssetAuditRow>& rows, EAssetAuditColumn column, bool ascending)
members.doc:
Stable in the sense that equal keys fall back to the name, so a re-sort
on the same column never reshuffles rows the reader was tracking.

members.name: FormatTimestamp
members.doc:
ISO-8601 in local time, or an empty string for a missing source. The
table and the CSV share it so an exported sheet sorts the same way the
panel did.

members.name: EscapeCsvField
members.doc:
RFC 4180: a field carrying a comma, a quote or a newline is quoted and
its quotes doubled. An asset path with a comma in it is rare and the
spreadsheet that silently shifted every column after it is not worth
the shortcut.

members.name: ToCsv
members.doc:
The rows exactly as the table shows them — same order, same columns.
An export that re-derives its own order answers a different question
than the screen the user was reading.

types.name: FUnresolvedAssetRef
types.doc:
Collects all asset file paths referenced by a set of scenes.
Component asset references are discovered reflection-driven: every
MOWO_ASSET_REF property on every registered component type is read
from the MDF node, so a new component with a new asset slot is picked
up with zero changes here. Materials/prefabs are followed recursively,
materials via a full UUID/AssetRef value walk (all texture slots plus
graph texture nodes). Used for selective build packing.
A reference the collector could not turn into a file on disk. Dropping
these in silence is how a broken reference reaches a shipped build: the
asset is simply absent from the archive and the runtime degrades at load.

members.name: reference
members.doc: the path or UUID exactly as it was written

members.name: referencedBy
members.doc: the scene/prefab/material it was found in

members.name: reason
members.doc: "file not found", "uuid not in registry", ...

members.name: Collect
members.signature: static std::unordered_set<std::string> Collect( const std::vector<std::string>& scenePaths, const std::string& assetsRoot, const AssetRegistry& registry, std::vector<FUnresolvedAssetRef>* outUnresolved = nullptr)

members.name: CollectAssets
members.signature: static std::unordered_set<std::string> CollectAssets( const std::vector<std::string>& assetPaths, const std::string& assetsRoot, const AssetRegistry& registry, std::vector<FUnresolvedAssetRef>* outUnresolved = nullptr)
members.doc:
Transitive closure of a set of ASSET paths (not scenes): materials
pull their texture/parent chains, prefabs their entity references,
plain assets just resolve. The per-sector closure used by the
streaming-aware cook layout.

types.name: EAssetRefKind
types.doc:
How strongly a reference binds. Hard means loading the referencer loads the
target as part of loading it at all — a material's textures, a prefab's
meshes. Soft means the reference is a path a component resolves later, so
the referencer loads without it and a miss degrades at runtime instead of
failing the load. The two cost completely different things in a cook and in
a delete, which is why they are drawn differently.

types.name: FAssetRefNode
types.doc:
Which side of the root a node sits on. Column 0 is the root itself,
negative columns are referencers (left), positive are dependencies (right).

members.name: isOverflow
members.doc:
A node that stands for the referencers/dependencies that did not fit
the per-column budget. The old viewer dropped them in silence, so a
material with 40 users looked identical to one with 24.

members.name: kind
members.doc:
The strongest edge reaching this node from the root's side. A node
pulled in by any hard edge is a hard cost even if a soft edge also
reaches it.

members.name: referencerDepth
members.doc:
Independent per direction: UE's viewer steps referencers and
dependencies separately because the interesting depth is rarely the
same on both sides.

members.name: typeFilter
members.doc:
Empty means every type. A node filtered out is not expanded either —
hiding a node but walking through it produced edges to nothing.

members.name: nameFilter
members.doc:
Case-insensitive substring over the file name. The root always
survives it, or the graph would have no anchor to read against.

members.name: restrictToLevel
members.doc:
"Show only this level's actors": the set of asset UUIDs the open scene
actually references. Off by default because an empty allow-set and a
disabled allow-set mean opposite things.

members.name: directDependencies
members.doc:
Direct (depth 1) counts, before filtering, so the header reads the
registry's truth rather than what survived the search box.

members.name: droppedNodes
members.doc:
Nodes the column budget refused. Surfaced in the toolbar and as the
overflow chips; a silent drop is the defect this replaces.

members.name: typesSeen
members.doc:
Every type the walk touched, filter or no filter. The type picker is
built from this: populating it from the FILTERED graph meant picking a
type emptied the picker of every other option, so there was no way back.

members.name: ResolveRoot
members.signature: static UUID ResolveRoot(const AssetRegistry& registry, const std::string& path)
members.doc:
Resolve a content path to its registry UUID, falling back to a file-name
match. A path handed over by the Content Browser can be absolute, VFS or
project-relative and only one of those is the registry's key.

members.name: Build
members.signature: static FAssetRefGraph Build(const AssetRegistry& registry, UUID root, const FAssetRefGraphOptions& options)
members.doc:
Breadth-first both ways from `root`, honouring the depth, budget and
filter options. Pure over the registry snapshot it reads.

members.name: LayoutColumns
members.signature: static void LayoutColumns(FAssetRefGraph& graph, float columnSpacing, float rowSpacing)
members.doc:
Column placement, split out so it can be checked without a widget:
column index drives X, row index drives a Y that centres each column on
the root's line. A column laid out from its own count rather than the
widest column would stagger the graph's centre line per column.

members.name: PassesTypeFilter
members.signature: static bool PassesTypeFilter(AssetType type, const std::vector<AssetType>& filter)
members.doc: Does `type` survive `filter`? Empty filter passes everything.

members.name: PassesNameFilter
members.signature: static bool PassesNameFilter(const std::string& name, const std::string& query)
members.doc: Case-insensitive substring, empty query passes everything.

types.name: EAssetSizeSource
types.doc:
Where a byte count came from. This is the whole point of the Size Map being
trustworthy: a treemap that mixes an exact cooked size with a guess and
labels neither teaches the reader to believe the guess.

members.name: Unknown
members.doc:
Nothing could be established. The tile is drawn, sized at zero, and
counted — an asset silently missing from a footprint total is how a
build ships 300 MB over budget with a green report.

members.name: ArchiveEntry
members.doc:
MEASURED. The cooked archive's table of contents, i.e. the exact bytes
this asset occupies in the shipped .meaf.

members.name: CookedHeader
members.doc:
MEASURED. A cooked .mtex header's totalDataSize — the exact resident
pixel bytes, read from the 64-byte header without touching the payload.

members.name: SourceFile
members.doc:
MEASURED, but of the SOURCE file, not of the cook. Correct as a number
and wrong as an answer to "how big will this ship" for anything that
gets recompressed, which is why it is labelled separately.

members.name: ResidentAsset
members.doc:
ESTIMATED. Asset::EstimatedMemoryUsage() on a resident asset — the same
figure the eviction policy runs on. MeshAsset's formula multiplies the
index count by the vertex stride, so mesh memory reads high.

members.name: depth
members.doc:
Depth from the root in the dependency walk. 0 is the root itself; the
treemap groups by it so a reader can tell "this asset" from "what it
drags in".

members.name: archivePath
members.doc:
Empty when no cooked archive was found, which is what turns every disk
figure into a source-file measurement instead of a cooked one.

members.name: projectRoot
members.doc:
Absolute project root, for turning the registry's project-relative
paths back into something stat() understands.

members.name: archivePath
members.doc: Explicit cooked archive. Empty means probe the conventional locations.

members.name: includeDependencies
members.doc:
Asset mode only: follow the dependency closure rather than sizing the
one asset. A shared asset is counted ONCE, the way a cook packs it.

members.name: includeSoft
members.doc:
Asset mode only: soft references are followed too by default, because
they still occupy the archive; turning this off answers "what does
loading this asset cost right now" instead.

members.name: FormatBytes
members.doc: 1.4 MB / 812 KB / 96 B. One decimal above KB, none below.

members.name: ProbeCookedArchive
members.doc:
The conventional cooked-archive locations, newest wins. Empty when none
exists, and the caller must then say so rather than pretending the
source sizes are cooked sizes.

members.name: BuildForAsset
members.signature: static FAssetSizeReport BuildForAsset(const AssetRegistry& registry, UUID root, const FAssetSizeOptions& options)
members.doc: Total footprint of one asset plus (by default) everything it drags in.

members.name: BuildForFolder
members.signature: static FAssetSizeReport BuildForFolder(const AssetRegistry& registry, const std::string& folder, const FAssetSizeOptions& options)
members.doc:
Every registered asset under `folder` (a project-relative prefix). No
closure: a folder view answers "what is in here", and following
dependencies out of the folder would double-count against its siblings.

members.name: InvalidateArchiveCache
members.doc:
Drop the cached cooked archive. The panel calls this when the user
re-cooks, or every reader keeps reporting the previous build's bytes.

types.name: EAssetFilterCategory
types.doc:
The content browser's filter chips. The order IS the chip order, and the
ordinal is what the browser shifts into its active-filter mask, so a new
category goes at the end rather than in the middle.

types.name: EAssetOrigin
types.doc:
How a file relates to the import pipeline. The browser needs all three
answers and used to derive each from its own extension list.

members.name: Imported
members.doc:
Authored in a DCC tool and copied into Content/ as-is. This IS the
asset here — import produces no derived container — so a source file is
reimportable and carries a type label of its own.

members.name: Produced
members.doc:
A container the engine itself writes: a cooked twin or a binary asset
package (mesh, texture, sound...). Also reimportable, because the copy
inside Content/ can be replaced.

members.name: Authored
members.doc:
Authored in the editor and never imported from anywhere: materials,
prefabs, scenes, data assets. Reimport is meaningless for these.

members.name: Companion
members.doc:
Files the browser lists but the asset system does not own: C++ sources,
build scripts, a glTF's .bin blob.

types.name: FAssetDisplayInfo
types.doc:
The one place that decides what a file IS for display purposes: its type
label, its filter chip, whether Reimport applies, whether an OS handler can
open it, and whether the Import dialog accepts it.

Six lists used to answer these independently and they had drifted apart:
the type column called every importable format "<EXT> File" while the
filter chips routed the same file through the model list, Reimport was
greyed out for every .fbx in the project, and the Import button's file
dialog refused two formats drag-and-drop accepted. It lives in Game beside
FAssetActionPolicy for the same reason that one does — the editor is an
executable and nothing can link its decisions, so the self-test host can
only pin a rule that sits below it.

members.name: ImportableTextureExtensions
members.doc:
Texture formats the import pipeline accepts. `.dds` is here and `.psd` is
not, because the question is what `TextureImporter` can turn into an
asset, not what decodes for a thumbnail.

members.name: HasImportOptionsPage
members.doc:
Whether the Import dialog has an options page for this format. A `.dds`
arrives already compressed and already mipped, so every control the
texture page offers is a decision the file has made — showing it would be
a window on settings that cannot apply. Such a format still imports; it
just takes the copy path directly. Asking here rather than from a list
of its own is what stops this drifting from the list above again.

members.name: TextureExtensions
members.doc:
Formats that decode to a tile and a preview whether or not they can be
imported — the Textures chip has to claim all of them or a .tga sitting
in Content/ becomes unfilterable.

members.name: IsImportable
members.doc:
Everything the Import dialog and an OS drop accept. The Import button's
file-dialog filter is built from this same answer, so the two gestures
can no longer disagree about a format.

members.name: ImportFileDialogPatterns
members.doc:
"*.png;*.jpg;…" for a native file dialog, in one place so the dialog can
never offer less than the drop handler takes.

members.name: IsReimportable
members.doc:
Reimport re-reads the file the asset was made from. That applies to
anything that arrived through the importer — which is every source
format, not only the containers the editor produces. While this
answered on containers alone the context menu showed a disabled Reimport
on every model in the project, and the needs-reimport badge, which asks
the same question, never appeared for one either.

members.name: HasExternalHandler
members.doc:
A file the OS has an application for, offered as "Open Externally". Only
formats a viewer on a stock machine actually opens — a cooked model would
launch whatever last claimed the extension, which is nothing.

members.name: TypeLabel
members.doc:
The type column. A source format names the asset it becomes, because
that is what it IS in this pipeline — a `.fbx` under Content/ is the
static mesh, not a file that happens to sit next to one.

members.name: TypeLabelDetail
members.doc:
The format a label came from, for the tooltip that used to be the only
place an author could learn which exporter wrote a mesh. Empty for
anything the label already names exactly.

types.name: AssetHandle
types.doc:
AssetHandle<T> — wrapper around Ref<T> that supports pending UUID resolution.
An asset handle can be in one of three states:
1. Empty — no UUID, no asset
2. Pending — has UUID, asset not yet loaded/resolved
3. Ready — has a valid Ref<T> to the loaded asset

Usage:
AssetHandle<TextureAsset> handle(someUUID);  // pending
handle.Resolve(assetManager);                 // try to resolve
if (handle.IsReady()) { handle->DoSomething(); }

types.name: AssetManager
types.doc:
Base AssetManager providing UUID-based asset cache and retrieval.
Subclassed by EditorAssetManager (scan/import) and RuntimeAssetManager (packed).

members.name: Get
members.doc: Singleton access

members.name: TryGet
members.doc: out-of-line; reading s_instance

members.name: SetInstance
members.doc:
from a consumer TU across the
MowoEngine.Game.dll boundary as
an inline triggers a dllimport
mismatch on the static storage.

members.name: Initialize
members.doc: Lifecycle

members.name: Update
members.doc:
Called once per frame: runs the eviction tick. Subclasses doing
their own per-frame work (GPU uploads) must call the base.

members.name: GetGpuUploadBudgetPerFrame
members.doc:
Max GPU uploads (CreateGPU calls) a subclass Update should drain per
frame; <= 0 means unbounded. Backed by the `asset.UploadsPerFrame`
cvar so a burst of finished async imports is time-sliced instead of
hitching the frame that receives them all.

members.name: SetMemoryBudget
members.doc:
The budget follows `asset.MemoryBudgetMB` whenever that cvar changes (0 =
keep the current one); FQualityAutoTier::ResolveDeviceBudgets claims it
from the device's VRAM. A direct SetMemoryBudget stands until the cvar
next moves.

members.name: RefreshMemoryEstimates
members.doc:
Re-reads every cached asset's estimate. An entry's size was captured
when it was cached — for a mesh, before its GPU buffers existed, so it
counted 0 for the rest of its life. EvictionTick refreshes on its own
every few frames; a caller that needs the number now asks here.

members.name: TouchAsset
members.doc: Bump the LRU stamp (GetAsset does this automatically).

members.name: PinAsset
members.doc: Pinned assets are never auto-evicted (UI atlases, always-resident).

members.name: UnloadAsset
members.doc:
Explicit unload: DestroyGPU + Unload + drop from the cache.
Fails (false) when something besides the cache still holds a ref —
yanking GPU resources from under a live user is a crash, not a
cleanup.

members.name: UnloadAssetsInSet
members.doc: Bulk variant for streaming sector unload.

members.name: ReleaseUnreferencedSince
members.doc:
Closing a level or an asset editor freed nothing: everything it loaded
stayed cached until usage crossed the whole budget (measured: three asset
editors 3.06 -> 4.32 GB private, 4.17 GB after closing them). The host
calls this a few updates after a document closed: it unloads every
unpinned asset nothing outside the cache holds and nobody touched since
`frame`. Components keep raw pointers into assets, so the host touches
whatever its still-open documents use first. Returns how many unloaded.

members.name: GetFrameCounter
members.doc: Update() count, the clock lastAccessFrame and the sweeps above run on.

members.name: GetAsset
members.doc: Get an asset by UUID. Returns null if not loaded.

members.name: GetAsset
members.signature: template<typename T> Ref<T> GetAsset(UUID id) const
members.doc: Get a typed asset by UUID.

members.name: GetAssetByPath
members.signature: template<typename T> Ref<T> GetAssetByPath(const std::string& path)
members.doc: Get a typed asset by source path.

members.name: RequestAssetAsync
members.doc:
The one load-by-path verb a caller below the editor/runtime split can
use: hands back the asset only when it is fully resident, otherwise
starts (or continues) loading it off the calling thread and returns
null. Poll it — the frame it returns non-null is the frame to use the
asset. Repeat calls for one path coalesce into one load. The base
only probes the cache, which is what a bare manager in a test wants.

members.name: ResolveMaterialTextures
members.doc:
Bind a material's texture slots from wherever the caller is — a mesh
applying its authored slot materials does it on the main thread, inside
the GPU drain. The base resolves them now, which is what a packaged
game with cooked textures wants; the editor imports what is missing in
the background and binds each slot as its texture lands, instead of
decoding every slot of every material in the one frame a model finishes.

members.name: IsImportInFlight
members.signature: virtual bool IsImportInFlight(const std::string& sourcePath) const
members.doc:
True while `sourcePath` is being imported in the background — queued,
parsing, or uploading. A big model takes seconds, and a tile that looks

types.name: FAssetPackageMigration
types.doc:
Two migrations (ROADMAP §23 D5 as amended 2026-10-01, §23.6, §23.8 step 8).

RenameLegacyExtensions — every project, every open: each file under
Content/ spelled the way an older engine wrote it moves to its type's own
extension (Core/FileTypes.h): .mdfmat -> .mat (.matinst when it has a
parent), .marcui -> .ui, .mtheme -> .theme, a generic .masset/.mdf package
-> the extension of the class in its summary, a level -> .mmap (single
file; a package project converts it instead), "<level>.sectors.mdf" ->
"<level>.sectors". The content is not touched.

Migrate — the text types into packages, for a project on the package
format: Material/Material Instance/Prefab/VisualScripting/UI files that do not lead
with a summary are wrapped in place under their own extension, a level
becomes a World package plus one .actor file per actor under
__ExternalActors__/<Level>/, and every other text asset type is wrapped in
place with its file-type row's name as its class, its sidecar left beside
it (MdfDocument::Root() steps over the summary, so its loaders read it as
before).

Each file keeps the UUID its .mdfmeta sidecar held, so every registry
reference by id survives; every path reference survives through an asset
redirect old -> new in Config/Redirects.ini and the quoted references under
Content/ are rewritten. Originals a conversion replaces move, never get
deleted, to Saved/MigratedSources/<same path>; a rename that would land on
an existing file is skipped and reported.

Removal date: 2027-04-19 for RenameLegacyExtensions and the legacy spellings it reads.

text assets in packages, and every open migrates any legacy file that
arrived since (a merge, a copy from another project). Below it the project
stays on the legacy files until someone migrates it on purpose.

types.name: FAssetRedirectFixup
types.doc:
"Fix Up Redirectors" — UE's operation, same purpose.

A redirect keeps an old path resolving after a rename, but it is a
permanent indirection: the scene on disk still names a file that is not
there. This pass rewrites those path strings to the new location and then
retires the redirect, so the project ends up with no indirection left.

The rewrite is deliberately textual and anchored on the surrounding quotes,
which is what makes it safe on hand-authored MDF: only a COMPLETE quoted
value can match (never a substring of a longer path), and the file's
formatting and comments are untouched — reparsing and re-emitting the
document would drop every comment in it.

Retiring is the dangerous half and is therefore evidence-based: a redirect
is dropped only once every file that could name it was actually examined.
It used to be dropped whenever no file the pass CHOSE to look at named it,
and the pass chose by a hand-written list of fourteen extensions — so a
reference living in a .msoundcue or a .mmontage had its redirect retired
underneath it, turning a working indirection into a dangling path while the
panel reported success.

members.signature: static FAssetRedirectFixupResult Run(const std::string& rootDirectory, AssetRegistry& registry)
members.doc:

recompute; a hash mismatch means the source genuinely changed → reimport

reconcile stats the sidecar first and, when it and the source are both
unchanged, never opens it — parsing every `.mdfmeta` of a 10k-asset
project on every launch was what UE's cached registry avoids. 0 = never
read, so the next reconcile parses it once and records this.

every existing caller that walks `dependencies` still sees every edge —
splitting the list would have quietly narrowed delete-safety, which is
the one query that must stay conservative. A registry written before
this field loads with it empty, i.e. every edge hard, which is the safe
reading of unknown.

G1 batch — parameters ride EXISTING node fields so serialization
stays untouched: Power exp = scalar (fallback when pin 1 unbound),
Clamp min/max = panSpeed.xy, Rotator speed(rad/s) = scalar,
TilingOffset tiling = panSpeed / offset = color.xy,
ValueNoise scale = scalar.

members.name: WorldPosition
members.doc:
G4: world-space position of the evaluated point — pixel stage reads
the interpolated WorldPos, the vertex stage the pre-offset vertex.

members.name: CustomHLSL
members.doc:
G1: user-authored HLSL (UE Custom node). The code body rides the
existing paramName string field (serialization untouched); it becomes
float4 MatCustom_<id>(float4 In0..In3, FMaterialInputs In) { <code> }
— write a `return`, read the four inputs and any FMaterialInputs
field. Never constant-folds; compile errors surface at cook with the
usual warn-and-fall-back-to-uber path.

members.name: VertexColor
members.doc:
G1: the mesh's per-vertex colour, interpolated. Live in every pass the
graph runs in (GBuffer, forward, masked shadow depth, velocity/WPO);
post-domain materials have no geometry and read white. Folds to white
too, so a graph that only multiplies by it is identity by default.

members.name: MakeMaterialAttributes
members.doc:
Layered materials (UE's material layers). These two node kinds carry a
whole surface along the wire instead of a float4 — a "layer bus". A
MakeMaterialAttributes packs the seven PBR channels into one; a
LayerBlend crossfades two of them under a mask, and chaining blends
stacks arbitrarily many layers. Every layer compiles into the SAME
per-material shader (one draw, one pipeline, no extra push bytes and no
descriptor churn) — the whole point of the feature is that N layers
cost one pass, not N.

The two buses are NOT interchangeable: a float4 wired into a layer pin,
or a layer wired into a float4 pin, is refused at compile time rather
than silently coerced. Coercion would produce a material that renders
plausibly and wrongly, which is the failure this rejection exists to
prevent.

Fields reused so serialization stays untouched: MakeMaterialAttributes
takes its unconnected-pin fallbacks from the same out*/color fields the
Output node uses; LayerBlend's `scalar` is the height-blend transition
width in height units (only read when the Height pin is connected).

members.name: MaterialFunctionCall
members.doc:
Material functions (UE's MaterialFunction). A call node names a
`.mmatfunc` asset by path (functionPath) and exposes one input pin per
Function Input node the function declares, in that function's node
order; its single output is the function's Function Output. The call is
INLINED at compile time — MaterialGraph::Resolve splices the function's
nodes into the caller with fresh ids and rewires the pins — so the
emitter, the fold and the WPO bound walk never see a call at all and a
function costs exactly what its body costs. Recursion (a function that
reaches itself through any chain of calls) is refused with an error
that names the cycle; without that check the resolver would expand
forever.

Inside a function: FunctionInput carries the pin name in paramName, its
unconnected-caller default in `color` (a scalar input reads .x) and its
type in scalarPin; FunctionOutput takes the result on slot 0 and names
it in paramName. Reached outside a function (the function editor's own
compile) an input reads its default and an output passes through.

members.name: StaticSwitch
members.doc:
Static switches (UE's StaticSwitchParameter). A StaticSwitch picks
True (slot 0) or False (slot 1) at COMPILE time from the StaticBool
wired into its Value pin (slot 2), or from its own boolValue when the
pin is unwired. The unselected branch is never visited: it emits no
code, takes no texture slot and no parameter lane. Every NAMED
StaticBool is one permutation axis — 2^N shader permutations, each
its own source and hash, bounded by r.Material.MaxStaticPermutations.
A material instance overrides the bool by name and thereby selects
its permutation. An unnamed StaticBool is a constant, not an axis.

members.name: SubstrateSlab
members.doc:
Substrate: a second BSDF slab layered over the material's own surface.
A slab is albedo / F0 / roughness / normal / coverage, and layering one
over another is what the fixed shading models cannot express — each of
them spends the single custom G-Buffer scalar on a different thing, so
clear-coat-over-cloth has nowhere to live.

Slice 1 encodes exactly two slabs and the bottom one IS the ordinary
surface (RT0/RT1), so this node authors the TOP slab. There is still no
VERTICAL stacking node: with two encodable slabs and the bottom one taken,
stacking two authored slabs needs three and every use would be a compile
error. That waits on the payload target —
Documentation/ROADMAP.md §12.4.

Coverage/Roughness/F0 are pins; the albedo is a two-bit codebook on the
node (maskChannel) because sixteen bits cannot hold an independent RGB.
The slab shares the base slab's normal for the same reason.

members.name: SubstrateBlend
members.doc:
Two slab definitions crossfaded under a mask, resolving to ONE slab
before the encode. This is the side-by-side case, not the vertical one:
its output is a single slab by construction, so it cannot produce a stack
that does not fit and needs no extra G-Buffer bits. What it buys is a coat
whose CHARACTER varies across the surface and not only its thickness — ice
on the ledges and powder in the crevices of one rock, wax on a jacket's
shoulders and bare fuzz elsewhere — which today needs two materials and a
mesh split.

The albedo codebook entry is the one thing it cannot blend: the mode is
two bits baked into the shader as a define, so the emitter refuses a blend
whose two slabs disagree about it rather than silently keeping one.

members.name: SceneDepth
members.doc:
Scene inputs (UE's SceneDepth / CustomDepth / CustomStencil): the scene's
device depth, the custom depth pass's depth and its stencil value at the
evaluated pixel. Pin 0 is an optional screen UV (defaults to the
pixel's own). Live in the post-process domain, where the pass binds the
three targets; the surface domains carry no frame block for them and
read zero. Fold to zero — a screen-space value has no constant.

types.name: FSubstrateCodec
types.doc:
The two-slab G-Buffer codec, mirrored from Engine/Shaders/Private/Lighting/
Substrate.hlsli. Slab 0 is the ordinary G-Buffer; this describes slab 1,
which rides the sixteen bits the tier-7 escape frees from clear-coat duty.
The shader and this struct are pinned against each other by the
substrate-codec-test row — a bit layout with two writers and no test is how
the anisotropy nibble drifted before it was centralised.

members.name: ExtendedSlot
members.doc:
Tier 7's low five bits name an extended slot; slot 1 is Eye, so
Substrate takes slot 2 and shading-model id 9. Renderer/Material.h has
no EShadingModel entry for it yet (that header is outside the material
path), so this is where the reservation lives.

members.name: MaxSlabs
members.doc:
Two slabs, fixed. Not a budget knob yet: widening it needs a G-Buffer
target, which is a renderer-owned change (plan §2).

members.name: eyeIrisTint
members.doc:
Eye (extended shading model 8). Unlike every field above these never
become a G-Buffer lane: the renderer routes them into the frame's
surface-parameter record that an escaped pixel's RT3 index names, which
is the only reason a model needing a per-pixel iris normal could ship at
all. They are deliberately NOT part of the emitted source, so retuning an
eye never recompiles its shader.

members.name: eyeGazeAxis
members.doc:
The per-draw half of the same record: the gaze axis the renderer rotates
by each draw's model matrix, plus the iris mask, limbal ring, iris lobe
and caustic that ride it. Every default is the inert one from
FEyeSurfaceParams, so a graph that authors them and a graph that does
not describe the same eye.

members.name: eyePerDrawAuthored
members.doc:
False until the graph actually carries the six fields above — the state
of every graph written before they had pins, and of every graph nobody
has touched them on. Those fields were `.mdfmat`-only for a release, so
compiling the defaults over them unconditionally would straighten a
hand-authored stare on the next unrelated graph edit; while this is
false the compiler leaves the material's own values alone.

members.name: domain
members.doc: 0 = Surface, 1 = PostProcess (G6), 2 = Decal (a projector's graph: BaseColor/Opacity/Normal/Metallic/Roughness), 3 = LightFunction (Emissive is the light's filter, evaluated over the projected UV)

members.name: maxWpo
members.doc:
Authored ceiling on |World Position Offset| in world units (0 = off).
Baked into the emitted vertex evaluator as a magnitude clamp — every
pass (GBuffer, shadow, velocity, forward, meshlet) evaluates the same
clamped offset, so tightening the derived cull bound to min(derived,
maxWpo) can never cull geometry the shader still displaces. The one
way to re-arm the geometric kills on a graph whose derived bound is
the unbounded sentinel. Participates in the shader hash (it changes
the emitted code), like every other Output-node constant.

members.doc:
MaterialFunctionCall: the `.mmatfunc` this call inlines, as the path

for the shipped set, a project-relative path for the project's own).

StaticBool: the switch's default. StaticSwitch: the value used when the

members.signature: static const char* InputPinName(MatNodeType type, uint32_t slot)

Label for one input pin. It lives next to InputCount because the two
have to grow together: the material editor keeps its own copy of this
table, whose default arm labels any slot it has not been taught with
the last name in its list — a wrong label rather than a missing one.

members.name: IsAttributeNode
members.doc:
Whether a node kind carries a layer bus (FMaterialAttributes) rather
than a float4. Mixing the two is a compile error, not a coercion.

members.name: IsSubstrateNode
members.doc:
Whether a node kind carries a Substrate slab. A third bus, kept apart
from the layer bus for the reason the two exist separately at all: a
horizontal layer blend crossfades seven PBR channels, a slab blend
crossfades three slab fields, and a wire that could be either would
compile and render plausibly and wrongly.

members.name: SubstrateAlbedoMode
members.signature: uint32_t SubstrateAlbedoMode(uint64_t nodeId, uint64_t& mismatchNode) const
members.doc:
The albedo codebook entry a slab subtree resolves to, following blends
down to their inputs. mismatchNode receives the id of the first blend
whose two sides disagree (kNoErrorNode when they all agree) — the mode is
two bits baked into the shader as a define, so a disagreement is a hard
limit and not something to average. Shared with the editor so the
diagnostic and the compile error can never drift apart.

members.name: FoldSubstrateTop
members.signature: uint32_t FoldSubstrateTop(uint64_t nodeId, bool& outVaries) const
members.doc:
The authored slab reduced to ONE packed G-Buffer word, or 0 when it does
not reduce (outVaries set). Two consumers cache a single answer per
surface rather than shading per pixel — the GI surface cache stores one
colour per card texel, and the ray-traced hit shading blends against that
cache — so both need a slab that is constant over the material. A graph
whose coverage rides a texture has no such word, and answering 0 there
leaves those two paths shading the base surface exactly as they did
before Substrate existed. That is a visible gap, not a silent one: the
material editor says so on the node, because an average coat invented
here would make a snow line bounce snow-coloured light into the crevices
it does not reach.

refusal raised inside a body can be pointed at the call. Returns false

does not author fields), and it is refused outright on a material that
has a parent: a graph is a ROOT material's authoring surface, an instance

types.name: MaterialGraph::ShaderStats
types.doc:
Offline HLSL codegen. EmitHLSL walks the output node's connected inputs
and emits a self-contained material function
(FMaterialOutputs EvaluateMaterial(FMaterialInputs)) into the same
template the GBuffer material path would #include. Real per-graph shader
variant compilation through DXC is not wired at runtime — this is the
authored artifact the cook would compile. EstimateStats returns the
instruction/sampler counts the editor shows.

types.name: MaterialGraph::FGraphParam
types.doc:
Compiled-material emission (the path `mbt` actually compiles, unlike
the free-standing EmitHLSL preview): texture nodes are assigned the
GBuffer material descriptor slots 0..7 in first-use order (deduped by
texture UUID), and the emitted code samples the MatGraphTexN/
MatGraphSampN aliases GBufferFill.hlsl defines under MATERIAL_GRAPH —
so the per-material shader keeps the exact pipeline layout of the
uber-shader and only the evaluation differs. Textures carries the
UUID for each used slot, in slot order; the renderer binds them into
the material descriptor set in the same order. Hash is FNV-1a of the
emitted source — the shader's stable identity for the cook, the cache
and the runtime lookup ("Materials/<hash-hex>").
R4: a NAMED Scalar/Vector parameter no longer constant-folds into the
source — it compiles to a read of a parameter lane the renderer feeds
per draw, so changing the value never recompiles the shader. Unnamed
param nodes keep folding (they are constants with a param-shaped node).

Lane layout. A graph whose parameters fit the ORIGINAL four-lane block
keeps that block's exact packing — vectors take whole lanes from the
front, scalars pack four per lane from the BACK — and reads them as
In.Params[lane]; its emitted source is byte-identical to what it was
before the ceiling was lifted, so every cooked blob, committed sidecar
and shader hash stands. A graph that does not fit takes the WIDE
layout: vectors from the front, scalars four per lane immediately
after them, up to kGraphParamLanesMax lanes; lanes 4 and up read
MatGraphParamsExt[lane - 4], a static array the emitted source declares
(zero unless the pass template fills it), and the source announces its
width with `#define MATERIAL_GRAPH_PARAM_LANES <n>` so the templates
and the upload can size their copy by the graph instead of by four.
The instance override path addresses lanes by name -> (lane, comp)
through this table, never by position.

members.name: wpoBound
members.doc:
Conservative interval bound on |EvaluateWorldPositionOffset| in world
units, evaluated under the vertex-stage input contract (UV/normal/
view read zero, vertex color in [0,1], time unbounded but folded
through sin/saturate/noise). The meshlet task stage inflates its
cluster cull spheres by this so per-cluster frustum/Hi-Z kills stay
sound under displacement; kWpoBoundUnbounded means the subtree could
not be bounded (e.g. it scales with WorldPosition) and every
geometric kill must be skipped instead. 0 when the graph has no WPO.
An authored Output-node maxWpo (> 0) tightens this to min(derived,
maxWpo) — sound because the same value is baked into the evaluator
as a magnitude clamp, so no pass can displace past it.

members.doc:

consumers that cache one answer per surface instead of shading per

both of them rendered before Substrate existed; substrateVaries says
whether that 0 means "none authored" or "authored, but it moves per
pixel and those paths cannot carry it".

types.name: MediaSourceAsset
types.doc:
MediaSourceAsset (.mmedia) — a clip plus how it should play, the way UE's
MediaSource + MediaPlayer settings pair.

FMediaPlayer::Open already takes a path, so why an asset: a bare path is not
a reference. It cannot be renamed with a redirector, it does not appear in
the dependency graph, and the cook has no way to know a movie is used — so a
packaged build ships with the cutscene missing and nothing says so until a
player reaches it. Naming the clip through an asset puts it on the same
footing as a texture or a mesh.

The playback settings live here rather than at each call site because they
belong to the CLIP: a looping ambient screen and a one-shot cutscene want
different answers, and the answer should travel with the content instead of
being re-decided by whoever opens it.

order (volume only sticks once a stream exists, i.e. after Open).
Returns false when the clip fails to open.

a small pool of dedicated loader threads (`editor.AsyncImportThreads`;
NOT JobSystem/FTaskGraph pool workers — a parse fans texture/LOD/meshlet
work out to the pool, so a pool worker would deadlock), highest priority
first, and NEVER touches the GPU queue; GPU resource creation is drained
on the MAIN thread in Update(), time-sliced. Two spellings of one file
never parse at once. The callback fires on the main thread once the asset
is fully GPU-ready (or with a null asset on failure). Requests for the
same path are coalesced — one import, all callbacks fire — and a repeat
at a higher priority moves a still-queued import up. The
`editor.SyncImport` cvar forces the legacy synchronous path.

types.name: HiZPyramid
types.doc:
A mip chain of max-depth images. mips[0] is the finest (the GPU
readback); each coarser level is a 2x2 max-reduction. Sampling picks
the level where the query rectangle covers ~one texel, then maxes the
2x2 neighbourhood — the standard Hi-Z lookup.

members.signature: void Build(const float* finest, int w0, int h0)

members.signature: float MaxOverRect(float u0, float v0, float u1, float v1) const
members.doc:
Maximum depth over a screen-space rectangle given in UV [0,1].
Picks the mip where the rect spans ~1 texel so only a 2x2 lookup is
needed, then maxes that neighbourhood. Returns 1.0 (far → never
occludes) for an invalid pyramid or empty rect.

types.name: FHiZOcclusion
types.doc:
Project a world-space bounding sphere (treated conservatively as its
enclosing AABB cube) through viewProj to a screen-space UV rectangle
and the NEAREST NDC depth. Returns false — meaning "do not cull" — if
any corner is at/behind the camera (w <= 0), where the projection is
unreliable. viewProj follows the engine convention: clip = viewProj *
(corner, 1), NDC = clip.xyz / clip.w, UV = ndc.xy * 0.5 + 0.5.

members.signature: static bool SphereOccluded(const HiZPyramid& hiz, const Vec3& center, float radius, const Mat4& viewProj, float bias = HIZ_OCCLUSION_BIAS)
members.doc:
Is the sphere occluded by the Hi-Z? Conservative: the sphere's nearest
depth must clear the farthest visible surface in its screen rect by
`bias` (a small slack that absorbs reprojection / quantisation, keeping
silhouettes from self-occluding). A fully off-screen rect is not
treated as occluded here — frustum culling owns that case.

members.name: SetAsyncDerivedData
members.doc:
Derived geometry data — the per-mesh SDF and GI card sets a model
straight from source needs and a cooked .mmodel already carries.

Both are cached in the DDC under a hash of the geometry itself, so a
model is baked once per content, not once per session. On a miss the
bake used to run inside LoadModelCPU, and the asset stayed unregistered
until it finished: two minutes for a 1,056-mesh scene in a Debug editor,
during which the file could not be opened, placed or even thumbnailed.

With async on (the editor turns it on) the model is usable as soon as
it is parsed; a background thread bakes, stores to the DDC, and
PumpDerivedData attaches the fields to the live meshes. Neither is
required to render — a mesh without them is simply left out of the SDF
field and gets the single whole-mesh card box meanwhile. Hosts that
leave it off (player, tests, cook) bake synchronously, as before.

types.name: FGiCardWarp
types.doc:
Where a card spends its texels ALONG its own surface. A card is one rectangle
over a whole box face, so a 40 m wall seen end-on used to be exactly as coarse
at the end the camera stands against as at the end forty metres away — the
per-face sizing that shipped picks how many texels the face gets, never where
they go. The warp redistributes the same texels toward the near end.

members.name: K
members.doc: 0 = uniform; the near-to-far texel density ratio is (K+1)^2

members.doc: warp the card's v axis instead of its u axis

members.name: Flip
members.doc: the dense end is at parameter 1, not 0

types.name: FGiCardFrame
types.doc:
One card box. The box is ORIENTED: `Axis` is its own orthonormal frame, so a
rotated wall gets a box the size of the wall instead of the world AABB that
contains it, which for a 45-degree wall is twice the area and five sixths of
it empty. Axis-aligned instances get the identity frame and cost nothing —
the packed rotation is then literally zero, which is what a zeroed record
already means.

The card-space convention and the warp are mirrored EXACTLY in
GI/GiSurfaceCache.hlsli. They have to be: the capture rasterizer derives its
projection from the record and the ray lookup inverts it, and a drift between
the two does not fail visibly — it samples the wrong texel of the right card.

members.doc: world position of the box corner card space measures from

lookup would disagree about.

and the hits nearest a card's edge miss it.

types.name: FGiCardResidencyRequest
types.doc:
One rank of the residency walk: the slot and the card edge each of its six
faces is asking for this frame.

`Set` names the card SET this slot belongs to — an instance whose mesh was
clustered offline holds several cards, and they are siblings: eviction takes
the whole set or none of it. Half a set is an instance answering lookups on
some of its surface and silently falling back to the flat voxel albedo on the
rest, with no way for a consumer to tell the two apart. The default means
"this slot is its own set", which is exactly the one-box-per-instance
behaviour, so a caller that knows nothing about sets is unchanged.

members.doc: tiles moved or were taken away — these must stop being published

members.doc: slots whose every face now holds the tile it asked for

members.doc: faces served at the minimum edge because the size they asked for did not fit

members.doc: rank the walk stopped at, or kNoRank

members.name: kDegradedCooldown
members.doc:

for its full size again. Without it the fallback is a treadmill in slow
motion: the degraded face asks for its real size next frame, evicts the
worst card to get it, fails anyway, degrades again, and the capture budget
goes to cards trading places exactly as it would have without the
stop-at-first-denial rule.

face whose coverage moved a mip step trades its tile; a request the atlas
cannot serve evicts the WORST-ranked card still holding space, never one
ranked above it and never a sibling of the request's own set; an eviction
takes the victim's WHOLE set, because a set's cards page together; and the
first request that still cannot be served — even at the minimum edge —

into a treadmill where every frame's capture budget is spent on cards
swapping places.

for SampleLocal; WorldScale converts the local (unit-space) distance back to
world units. WorldMin/Max is the padded field AABB transformed to world (the
spatial-cull box). Albedo carries the tint (rgb) + emissive scale (.a);
Emissive carries the emissive COLOUR (rgb, normalised to [0,1] — any excess
is folded into the scale by the caller) so the composite can keep the true
albedo instead of lerping the two into one purple float4.

types.name: FVirtualTextureTileFile
types.doc:
A cooked virtual-texture tile file (.mvtiles): every page of every mip of a
source image, already padded with its border ring and block-compressed, laid
out so one page is one contiguous range. The disk provider streams a page by
reading exactly that range (VFS::ReadFileRange — a native seek, or only the
archive blocks the range touches) and hands the blocks straight to the atlas,
which is created in the same BCn format: no decode on the CPU, and a quarter
(BC7) or an eighth (BC1) of the RGBA8 atlas's memory and upload bandwidth.

Layout: FHeader, then the tiles of mip 0 row by row, then mip 1, ... up to the
1x1 top mip. The page pyramid is VirtualTexturePageCache's: mip m has
max(1, pages >> m) pages per axis.

types.name: FMeshStreamingManager
types.doc:
Discrete-LOD residency for static meshes — the mesh half of the
texture-streaming pair (FTextureStreamingManager). The renderer's LOD
resolve notes the finest level each mesh was drawn at
(GPUMesh::NoteDesiredLOD); Update() evicts finer levels a mesh has not
needed for a hold window, restores them (byte-budgeted per call) the
moment a view wants them again, and force-coarsens the least-recently
promoted meshes while the resident pool exceeds the budget.

v1 keeps the CPU vertex/index copies for every registered level in
system memory and streams the GPU residency only — the copies are the
restore source, so re-admission never touches the filesystem. The
registration is per mesh (ModelResource registers static lit LOD-carrying
meshes without meshlets while r.MeshStreaming is on — the default — and a
host drives the manager); anything unregistered keeps the
everything-always-resident behaviour, as does an evicted level's draw —
GPUMesh accessors fall back to the finest still-resident level.

Get().Update(). Cleared with the scene teardown via Clear().

members.signature: void Register(const Ref<GPUMesh>& mesh, std::vector<LevelData> levels)
members.doc:

game thread it swapped a mesh's buffers while the rendering thread was
still recording the previous frame from them. Returns how many LOD
levels changed residency.
